note.explanation: Cells need a steady supply of usable energy. In this chapter, ATP links the energy released by respiration to the work cells perform, while photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose.
examples: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.
Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.
note.checkAnswer: ATP is the cell’s usable energy carrier; ADP can gain a phosphate group to become ATP.
note.simple: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose. Respiration releases energy from glucose, and ATP carries usable energy around the cell.
note.checkQuestion: What is the main purpose of cellular respiration?
note.title: Bioenergetics: energy in living things
steps: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy during photosynthesis.
Plants use carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen.
Respiration breaks down glucose and transfers some of its energy to ATP.
With oxygen, aerobic respiration produces much more ATP than anaerobic respiration.
Without enough oxygen, cells can use anaerobic respiration, which produces less ATP.
note.answer: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose, and cellular respiration releases energy from glucose for cell activities.

mcqs.stem: Q8.1. When we get energy from ATP, which bonds are broken?
rationales: Correct: energy is released when the terminal phosphate bond in ATP is broken.
Incorrect: C-H bonds are not the phosphate bonds broken when ATP releases energy.
Incorrect: C-N bonds are not the phosphate bonds broken when ATP releases energy.
Incorrect: C-O bonds are not the phosphate bonds broken when ATP releases energy.

mcqs.stem: Q8.2. Light reactions of photosynthesis occur in;
rationales: Incorrect: the plasma membrane is not the site of photosynthetic light reactions in plants.
Incorrect: the cytoplasm is not the site of photosynthetic light reactions in plants.
Incorrect: the stroma is where the light-independent reactions occur.
Correct: the thylakoid membranes contain the pigments and machinery for the light reactions.

mcqs.stem: Q8.3. Which type of chlorophyll is most common in plants?
rationales: Correct: chlorophyll a is the principal and most common photosynthetic pigment in plants.
Incorrect: chlorophyll b is an accessory pigment, not the most common type.
Incorrect: chlorophyll c is not the most common chlorophyll in plants.
Incorrect: chlorophyll d is not the most common chlorophyll in plants.

mcqs.stem: Q8.4. Which wavelengths of light are absorbed to maximum by chlorophylls?
rationales: Incorrect: green light is mostly reflected, rather than absorbed maximally.
Incorrect: green light is mostly reflected, rather than absorbed maximally.
Correct: chlorophyll absorbs light most strongly in the blue and red regions.
Incorrect: chlorophyll reflects much of the green light, which is why plants look green.

mcqs.stem: Q8.5. When yeast ferments glucose, the products are;
rationales: Correct: alcoholic fermentation in yeast produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.
Incorrect: yeast fermentation produces carbon dioxide as well as alcohol, not water as the stated product.
Incorrect: lactic acid is produced in lactic acid fermentation, not yeast fermentation.
Incorrect: carbon dioxide may be produced, but water is not the other product of yeast fermentation.

mcqs.stem: Q8.6. Where do the dark reactions of photosynthesis occur?
rationales: Correct: the light-independent reactions occur in the chloroplast stroma.
Incorrect: thylakoids are the site of the light reactions.
Incorrect: the outer membrane is not the site of the dark reactions.
Incorrect: in plants, the dark reactions take place in the chloroplast stroma, not the cytoplasm.

mcqs.stem: Q8.7. Which molecule donates electrons in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis?
rationales: Incorrect: NADPH carries electrons made available during the light reactions; it is not the initial electron donor.
Correct: water is split and donates electrons during the light-dependent reactions.
Incorrect: oxygen is released when water is split; it does not donate the electrons.
Incorrect: carbon dioxide is used in carbon fixation and is not the electron donor in the light reactions.

mcqs.stem: Q8.8. Which process in aerobic respiration produces the most ATP?
rationales: Incorrect: glycolysis produces only a small amount of ATP compared with the electron transport chain.
Incorrect: the Krebs cycle produces less ATP than the electron transport chain.
Correct: most ATP in aerobic respiration is produced by the electron transport chain.
Incorrect: fermentation is anaerobic and produces little ATP.

mcqs.stem: Q8.9. How many ATP molecules are the net profit from one glucose molecule during anaerobic respiration?
rationales: Correct: anaerobic respiration yields a net profit of 2 ATP molecules per glucose.
Incorrect: 4 ATP may be formed in glycolysis, but 2 ATP are used, giving a net profit of 2.
Incorrect: anaerobic respiration does not yield 12 ATP per glucose.
Incorrect: 36 ATP is associated with the much greater yield from aerobic respiration in the textbook account.

mcqs.stem: Q8.10. What is a common byproduct of anaerobic respiration in animal cells?
rationales: Incorrect: oxygen is required for aerobic respiration and is not the anaerobic byproduct asked for.
Incorrect: water is not the common anaerobic byproduct in animal cells.
Correct: lactic acid can form in animal cells when oxygen is insufficient.
Incorrect: carbon dioxide is produced in alcoholic fermentation and aerobic respiration, not as the common byproduct in animal cells here.

written.text: Q8.1. Write the importance of oxidation-reduction reactions.
written.finalAnswer: Oxidation-reduction reactions transfer electrons and release energy that cells can use to make ATP.

rubric.why: This identifies the electron transfer involved in oxidation-reduction reactions.
rubric.description: State that oxidation-reduction reactions involve electron transfer.
rubric.how: Mention the transfer of electrons between substances.

rubric.why: This connects these reactions to usable cellular energy.
rubric.description: Explain their importance in releasing energy for ATP formation.
rubric.how: State that released energy is used to make ATP or do cellular work.

modelAnswer: Oxidation-reduction reactions involve the transfer of electrons from one substance to another.
The energy released can be used by cells to make ATP.

written.text: Q8.2. What do ATP and ADP mean? What are the roles of these molecules for the cellular metabolism?
written.finalAnswer: ATP means adenosine triphosphate and ADP means adenosine diphosphate. ATP transfers usable energy for cellular activities; when its terminal phosphate is removed, ATP becomes ADP and releases energy. ADP can be converted back to ATP by gaining a phosphate group.

rubric.why: The full name distinguishes ATP from ADP and is a core factual point.
rubric.description: Give the meanings of ATP and ADP.
rubric.how: Write adenosine triphosphate and adenosine diphosphate.

rubric.why: This explains their linked role in energy transfer during metabolism.
rubric.description: State how ATP and ADP function in cellular metabolism.
rubric.how: Explain that ATP releases usable energy when a phosphate is removed and ADP can be recharged with phosphate.

modelAnswer: ATP means adenosine triphosphate; ADP means adenosine diphosphate.
ATP transfers usable energy to cellular activities when its terminal phosphate group is removed, forming ADP.
ADP gains a phosphate group and energy to become ATP again.

written.text: Q8.3. Write down the word equation for photosynthesis.
written.finalAnswer: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

rubric.why: These are the reactants in the word equation.
rubric.how: Write carbon dioxide and water.

rubric.why: These are the products and complete the equation.
rubric.description: Give the products in the correct equation.
rubric.how: Write glucose and oxygen on the products side.

modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

written.text: Q8.4. Why is chlorophyll important for photosynthesis?
written.finalAnswer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy needed for photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Chlorophyll's light-absorbing role is the key function asked for.
rubric.how: Say that chlorophyll absorbs or traps light energy.

rubric.why: This explains why absorbed light matters to the process.
rubric.description: Link the absorbed light energy to photosynthesis.
rubric.how: State that this energy powers photosynthesis.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
This energy is used to carry out photosynthesis.

written.text: Q8.5. How is oxygen produced during photosynthesis?
written.finalAnswer: Light energy splits water molecules during the light reactions, releasing oxygen.

rubric.why: Water is the source of oxygen released in photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Identify the source of the oxygen.
rubric.how: State that oxygen comes from water molecules.

rubric.why: Light-driven splitting explains how the oxygen is released.
rubric.description: Describe the process that releases oxygen.
rubric.how: Explain that light energy splits water, releasing oxygen.

modelAnswer: In the light reactions, light energy splits water molecules.
Oxygen is released as a product.

written.text: Q8.6. Which organisms carry out photosynthesis? Which cell organelle is responsible for the absorption of light for photosynthesis?
written.finalAnswer: Green plants, algae and some bacteria carry out photosynthesis; chloroplasts absorb light in plant cells.

rubric.why: Naming photosynthetic organisms answers the first part.
rubric.description: Name organisms that carry out photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Give examples such as green plants, algae or some bacteria.

rubric.why: The chloroplast is the light-absorbing organelle in plant cells.
rubric.how: Write chloroplast.

modelAnswer: Green plants, algae and some bacteria carry out photosynthesis.
In plant cells, chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and absorb light for photosynthesis.

written.text: Q8.7. State the main purpose of cellular respiration?
written.finalAnswer: The main purpose of cellular respiration is to release energy from glucose and transfer it to ATP for cellular activities.

rubric.why: The central purpose is releasing energy from food molecules.
rubric.how: Mention energy released from glucose or food.

rubric.why: The energy is captured in a usable form for the cell.
rubric.description: State how cells use the released energy.
rubric.how: Mention ATP or cellular activities.

modelAnswer: Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose.
Some of this energy is transferred to ATP for cellular activities.

written.text: Q8.8. State the equation (in words or symbols) for aerobic respiration.
written.finalAnswer: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

rubric.why: These are the reactants for aerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Write glucose and oxygen on the left side.

rubric.why: These are the products and energy yield of the process.
rubric.how: Write carbon dioxide, water and energy on the right side.

modelAnswer: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

written.text: Q8.9. Write a brief note on the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration.
written.finalAnswer: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration. It combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water, allowing the electron transport chain to continue and ATP to be produced.

rubric.why: Oxygen's position at the end of the electron transport chain is its key role.
rubric.description: State oxygen's role as final electron acceptor.
rubric.how: Identify oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

rubric.why: This links oxygen's role to water formation and continued ATP production.
rubric.description: Explain the consequence of oxygen accepting electrons.
rubric.how: Mention water formation or that electron transport and ATP production can continue.

modelAnswer: Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain.
It combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water, allowing the chain to continue and ATP to be produced.

written.text: Q8.10. Define anaerobic and aerobic respiration.
written.finalAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen; anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the absence of oxygen.

rubric.why: The presence of oxygen distinguishes aerobic respiration.
rubric.how: State that glucose is broken down in the presence of oxygen.

rubric.why: The absence of oxygen distinguishes anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: State that glucose is broken down without oxygen.

modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen.
Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the absence of oxygen.

written.text: Q8.11. What are the end products of anaerobic respiration in animals and yeast?
written.finalAnswer: In animals, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid; in yeast, it produces alcohol (ethanol) and carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: Lactic acid is the characteristic end product in animal cells.
rubric.how: Write lactic acid.

rubric.why: Yeast fermentation produces both alcohol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Write alcohol or ethanol and carbon dioxide.

modelAnswer: In animals, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid.
In yeast, it produces alcohol (ethanol) and carbon dioxide.

written.text: Q8.12. How do muscles respond to oxygen deficiency during intense exercise?
written.finalAnswer: When oxygen is insufficient, muscle cells respire anaerobically, producing lactic acid and only a small amount of ATP; lactic acid accumulation contributes to muscle fatigue.

rubric.why: The muscle's response to insufficient oxygen is anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Say that muscles respire anaerobically when oxygen is insufficient.

rubric.why: The product and its effect describe the consequence for muscles.
rubric.description: State a consequence of anaerobic respiration in muscle.
rubric.how: Mention lactic acid production or muscle fatigue.

modelAnswer: During intense exercise, oxygen may not reach the muscles in sufficient amounts.
Muscle cells then respire anaerobically, producing lactic acid and a small amount of ATP.
Lactic acid accumulation contributes to muscle fatigue.

written.text: Q8.13. List ways in which respiratory energy is used in the body.
written.finalAnswer: Respiratory energy is used for muscle contraction and movement, active transport, growth and repair, cell division, synthesis of molecules, and maintaining body temperature.

rubric.why: Muscle activity is a major use of energy from respiration.
rubric.description: Give examples of body processes using respiratory energy.
rubric.how: Name muscle contraction or movement and at least one other use.

rubric.why: Additional valid cellular or body uses complete the list.
rubric.how: List processes such as active transport, growth, repair, synthesis or temperature maintenance.

modelAnswer: Respiratory energy is used for muscle contraction and movement.
It is also used in active transport, growth and repair, cell division, synthesis of molecules and maintaining body temperature.

written.text: Q8.1. Explain ATP as a molecule that is the chief energy currency of all cells.
written.finalAnswer: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the chief energy currency of cells. It consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups. Energy is stored in its phosphate bonds. When the terminal phosphate bond is broken by hydrolysis, ATP becomes ADP and phosphate and usable energy is released for cellular activities. Energy from respiration can add phosphate to ADP to regenerate ATP.

rubric.why: This identifies ATP and its central role in cellular energy transfer.
rubric.description: Identify ATP as the cell's energy currency.
rubric.how: Give its full name and state that it carries or transfers usable energy.

rubric.why: The components explain ATP's molecular structure.
rubric.how: Name adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.

rubric.why: Breaking off the terminal phosphate explains energy release.
rubric.how: State that ATP loses its terminal phosphate and becomes ADP, releasing energy.

rubric.why: ATP's regeneration explains how the energy carrier is reused.
rubric.description: Explain ATP regeneration and its use.
rubric.how: State that energy enables ADP to gain phosphate and reform ATP for cell work.

modelAnswer: ATP means adenosine triphosphate and is the chief energy currency of cells.
It consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
Energy is associated with the bonds between its phosphate groups.
When the terminal phosphate bond is broken by hydrolysis, ATP forms ADP and phosphate and releases usable energy.
This energy is used for cellular activities such as movement, active transport and synthesis.
Energy from respiration can add phosphate to ADP to regenerate ATP.

written.text: Q8.2. Outline the processes involved in photosynthesis?
written.finalAnswer: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy in the thylakoids. Light reactions split water, releasing oxygen and producing energy-rich carriers. In the stroma, the dark reactions use carbon dioxide and these products to form glucose.

rubric.why: The organelle and light absorption establish where photosynthesis begins and its energy source.
rubric.description: State the site and light capture.
rubric.how: Mention chloroplasts and chlorophyll absorbing light.

rubric.why: The light reactions and water splitting account for oxygen release.
rubric.how: State that light reactions occur in thylakoids and split water, releasing oxygen.

rubric.why: This locates the carbon-fixing stage of photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Describe the dark reactions' site and role.
rubric.how: Say that dark reactions occur in the stroma and use carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: Glucose is the main food product made by the process.
rubric.description: State the outcome of the process.
rubric.how: Explain that the reactions use carbon dioxide and energy-rich products to form glucose.

modelAnswer: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells.
Chlorophyll in the thylakoids absorbs light energy.
During the light reactions, water is split; oxygen is released and energy-rich molecules are formed.
The dark reactions occur in the stroma and use carbon dioxide and products of the light reactions to make glucose.

written.text: Q8.3. Write a note on the intake of carbon dioxide and water by plants
written.finalAnswer: Carbon dioxide enters leaves through stomata by diffusion. Water is absorbed from the soil by root hairs and carried to the leaves through xylem vessels. Both substances are raw materials for photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Stomata provide the route for carbon dioxide to enter leaves.
rubric.how: State that carbon dioxide enters through stomata, usually by diffusion.

rubric.why: Root hairs absorb water from the soil.
rubric.how: State that roots or root hairs take up water from the soil.

rubric.why: The transport route explains how water reaches photosynthesising leaves.
rubric.description: State how water moves to the leaves.
rubric.how: Mention xylem vessels carrying water to the leaves.

rubric.why: This connects both inputs to the process in the question's context.
rubric.how: State that carbon dioxide and water are photosynthesis raw materials.

modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide from the air enters the leaf through small pores called stomata, mainly by diffusion.
Water is absorbed from the soil by root hairs.
It is carried from the roots to the leaves through xylem vessels.
Carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials used in photosynthesis.

written.text: Q8.4. Explain the types and importance of anaerobic respiration.
written.finalAnswer: Anaerobic respiration releases energy from glucose without oxygen. In animal muscle cells it produces lactic acid; in yeast it produces alcohol and carbon dioxide. It provides a small amount of ATP when oxygen is unavailable, allowing cells to continue essential activities; yeast fermentation is also useful in making bread and alcoholic drinks.

rubric.why: This defines the condition under which anaerobic respiration occurs.
rubric.how: State that glucose is broken down without oxygen.

rubric.why: This identifies one type and its products in animal cells.
rubric.description: Give the animal-cell type or product.
rubric.how: State that muscle cells produce lactic acid.

rubric.why: This identifies alcoholic fermentation and its products.
rubric.description: Give the yeast type and products.
rubric.how: State that yeast produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: Anaerobic respiration's energy yield explains its biological importance.
rubric.how: State that it supplies some energy or ATP when oxygen is unavailable.

rubric.why: A valid use shows the practical importance of yeast fermentation.
rubric.description: Give a useful application or further importance.
rubric.how: Mention bread-making or alcoholic-drink production.

modelAnswer: Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose without oxygen and releases only a small amount of energy.
In animal muscle cells, it produces lactic acid.
In yeast, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.
It supplies some ATP when oxygen is insufficient, enabling cells to continue activities.
Yeast fermentation is also used in making bread and alcoholic drinks.

written.text: Q8.5. Outline the mechanism of aerobic respiration.
written.finalAnswer: Aerobic respiration breaks down glucose in the presence of oxygen. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and forms pyruvate, a small amount of ATP and NADH. In the mitochondrion, pyruvate is further broken down and enters the Krebs cycle, releasing carbon dioxide and transferring energy to carriers. Electrons pass through the electron transport chain; oxygen is the final electron acceptor and water forms. Most ATP is produced in the electron transport chain.

rubric.why: This gives the overall process and its requirement.
rubric.how: State that glucose is broken down in the presence of oxygen.

rubric.why: Glycolysis is the first stage and locates the initial glucose breakdown.
rubric.how: Mention glycolysis in the cytoplasm and formation of pyruvate.

rubric.why: This accounts for further breakdown and carbon dioxide release.
rubric.how: Mention the Krebs cycle in mitochondria and carbon dioxide release.

rubric.why: The electron transport chain, oxygen and ATP production complete the mechanism.
rubric.description: Describe the final stage and energy outcome.
rubric.how: State that oxygen accepts electrons, water forms and most ATP is made in the electron transport chain.

modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and NADH.
Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is further broken down; the Krebs cycle releases carbon dioxide and transfers energy to carriers.
Electrons pass along the electron transport chain in the mitochondrion.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with hydrogen to form water.
Most ATP is produced during the electron transport chain.

written.text: Q8.6. Compare the processes of respiration and photosynthesis.
written.finalAnswer: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water and releases oxygen; it occurs in chloroplasts. Respiration breaks down glucose, usually using oxygen in aerobic respiration, to release energy as ATP and produces carbon dioxide and water; it occurs mainly in the cytoplasm and mitochondria. The products of one process are reactants for the other.

rubric.why: The photosynthesis inputs and product establish the first side of the comparison.
rubric.how: Explain that it uses carbon dioxide and water to form glucose.

rubric.why: Its energy source and cellular location distinguish photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Give photosynthesis energy source or site.
rubric.how: Mention light captured by chlorophyll and/or chloroplasts.

rubric.why: This states respiration's direction and purpose.
rubric.how: Explain that it breaks down glucose to release energy as ATP.

rubric.why: Respiration products and site provide a direct comparison.
rubric.how: Mention carbon dioxide and water and/or mitochondria.

rubric.why: The reciprocal relationship is an important concluding comparison.
rubric.description: State the relationship between the processes.
rubric.how: Explain that products of photosynthesis are used in respiration and vice versa.

modelAnswer: Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts; respiration takes place mainly in the cytoplasm and mitochondria.
Photosynthesis uses light energy, carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen.
Respiration breaks down glucose; aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases energy as ATP, carbon dioxide and water.
Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose, whereas respiration releases energy from glucose.
The products of photosynthesis are used in respiration, and the products of respiration can be used in photosynthesis.

written.text: Q8.1. How does the structure of ATP enable it to store and release energy efficiently?
written.finalAnswer: ATP consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups. Its phosphate groups are linked by bonds associated with readily transferable energy. Removing the terminal phosphate by hydrolysis forms ADP and inorganic phosphate and releases usable energy quickly. ATP is regenerated when energy is used to add phosphate to ADP, so it can be reused.

rubric.why: ATP's structure is the basis of how its phosphate groups store transferable energy.
rubric.how: Name adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.

rubric.why: This identifies the part of ATP involved in energy transfer.
rubric.description: Explain where transferable energy is associated.
rubric.how: Mention the bonds between phosphate groups, especially the terminal phosphate.

rubric.why: Breaking off the terminal phosphate explains rapid energy release.
rubric.how: State that hydrolysis removes the terminal phosphate, forming ADP and releasing energy.

rubric.why: Regeneration explains how ATP efficiently serves as a reusable energy carrier.
rubric.how: State that ADP gains phosphate using energy and is reused as ATP.

modelAnswer: ATP consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
The phosphate groups are joined by bonds associated with transferable energy.
Hydrolysis removes the terminal phosphate group, forming ADP and inorganic phosphate and releasing usable energy quickly.
Energy can be used to add phosphate back to ADP, regenerating ATP for repeated use.

examTips: Section A tests key facts such as sites of reactions, products and ATP yield; learn the correct term as well as the idea.
Short questions usually earn marks for a direct fact plus a linked explanation, so use precise words such as thylakoid, stroma, ATP and lactic acid.
For equations, put the correct reactants and products on opposite sides and include oxygen for aerobic respiration.
Long answers should be set out in ordered stages, with locations and products stated at each stage.
For comparisons, compare both processes point by point; do not describe only photosynthesis or only respiration.
In respiration questions, distinguish the small net anaerobic yield of 2 ATP from the much greater aerobic yield.

example.question: Q8.1. Explain ATP as a molecule that is the chief energy currency of all cells.
example.answer: ATP is the chief energy currency of cells: it releases usable energy when its terminal phosphate group is removed, and it can be regenerated from ADP.

explain.title: ATP transfers usable energy
explain.body: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) can release usable energy when its terminal phosphate group is removed, forming ADP. Cells use this energy for activities such as movement, active transport and building molecules. ADP can gain phosphate to become ATP again.

explain.title: Photosynthesis stores energy
explain.body: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light. Light reactions take place in thylakoids and split water, releasing oxygen. Dark reactions take place in the stroma and use carbon dioxide and energy-rich products to make glucose.

explain.title: Respiration releases energy
explain.body: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose and transfers some of its energy to ATP. Glycolysis begins in the cytoplasm. Aerobic respiration continues in mitochondria and produces most ATP through the electron transport chain.

explain.title: Oxygen makes aerobic respiration possible
explain.body: In aerobic respiration, oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain and water forms. Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.

explain.title: Anaerobic respiration yields less energy
explain.body: Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and yields a net 2 ATP per glucose. Animal cells produce lactic acid; yeast produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.

mistakes: Do not say chloroplast stroma is the site of light reactions: light reactions occur in thylakoids, while dark reactions occur in the stroma.
Do not say oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide; it is released when water is split.
Do not confuse the products of anaerobic respiration in animals (lactic acid) with those in yeast (alcohol and carbon dioxide).
Do not give 4 ATP as the net yield of anaerobic respiration: the net profit is 2 ATP per glucose.
Do not leave out oxygen from the aerobic respiration equation or put it in the anaerobic definition.
In ATP answers, explain both energy release (ATP to ADP) and regeneration (ADP to ATP).
